question: to the Commission Anthony Smith (The Left) Subject:

Cadmium in phosphate fertilisers is classified as definitely carcinogenic and builds up in the soil and the food chain, where it will remain permanently. According to the French Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health and Safety (ANSES), almost half of French adults already exceed the health reference thresholds and young children are particularly at risk. Phosphate fertilisers alone are responsible for more than 80 % of the cadmium entering French agricultural soil. The Marne department and the Grand Est region, which form France’s second-largest beet-producing basin, are directly affected by this issue, due to such fertilisers being heavily used in the area. Regulation (EU) 2019/1009 limits the cadmium content in phosphate fertilisers to 60 mg/kg P₂O₅, but France currently benefits from a derogation and applies a threshold of 90 mg/kg – well above the harmonised ceiling set by the regulation. Meanwhile, ANSES recommends that the cadmium content be no more than 20 mg/kg. Article 49 of the regulation provides for a review of the limit value by 16 July 2026. In view of the above: 1.
What is the state of play regarding the review provided for in Article 49 of Regulation (EU) 2019/1009, and will the deadline of 16 July 2026 be met?
Does the Commission intend to bring the future EU threshold into line with the 20 mg/kg recommended by ANSES?

How does it justify Member States such as France continuing to apply thresholds above the harmonised limits that it itself has laid down, and does it intend to put an end to this as part of the review?
answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (14.8.2026) The Commission recognises the risks to human health and the environment associated to the presence of cadmium in fertilisers. The evaluation of Regulation (EU) 2019/10091 in accordance with Article 49 of this Regulation, including the review of cadmium limits, is being finalised. The Commission plans to submit its report to the Council and the European Parliament in the third quarter of 2026. Cadmium in soil and crops is a complex issue influenced by local conditions, agricultural practices and long-term accumulation patterns. The feasibility to reduce the maximum values of cadmium in phosphate fertilisers to a lower appropriate level must take into account available cadmium-removal technologies and scientific evidence on cadmium exposure and accumulation in the environment, on impacts on health and the environment (in particular in the context of soil and climatic conditions), as well as socio-economic factors such as security of supply and fertiliser affordability. This assessment will be based on available evidence, including the work published by the French Agency for Food, Environmental and Occupational Health and Safety (ANSES). Regulation (EU) 2019/1009 provides for optional harmonisation which allows Member States to apply their national law to fertilising products that are not CE-marked in accordance with the EU rules. Manufacturers can choose between complying with Regulation (EU) 2019/1009 and obtaining single market access via the CE marking and placing their product on the market under national rules and cross borders based on mutual recognition. The Commission will assess the feasibility and possible impacts of full harmonisation of the rules for inorganic fertilisers, as stated in the Fertilisers Action Plan2.
